summary:
No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding is documented for Córdoba. A trans visitor here stands under the national Colombian framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America, and is assessed against the national position on lethal violence rather than against any local deviation.

Nationally, nothing about being trans is criminalised. Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition: since a rule change approved in June 2015, the sex marker on government-issued identification is changed by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

The enforcement gap is severe. Monitoring bodies recorded 270 LGBTIQ+ killings in 2025, one every 32 hours and a 63% increase on the 164 recorded in 2024. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. One count put the number of trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 at 13.

Lethal anti-trans violence occurs in ordinary urban settings, in daylight, and can leave the perpetrator free. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín on 4 April 2025; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". Solidarity events were held in several cities.

The sharpest territorial risk sits where armed groups operate. In Caquetá, flyers on the street and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets and announced "social cleansing" campaigns against "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots", with a further wave threatened. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; another trans woman reported that a friend was killed. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Trans women in Caquetá reported few options beyond sex work, and Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men.

The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that widespread discrimination and violence must be addressed urgently as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against LGBT people has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Discrimination constrains trans women's livelihoods to hairdressing or sex work, which narrows the options for a trans person stranded by threats and is a recurring feature of the displacement reports from both departments. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023.

The structural risk in Córdoba resembles the armed-actor pattern documented elsewhere in Colombia rather than a distinct departmental regime: flyers, kill lists and ultimatums issued by groups controlling territory, followed by flight. Comparable urban cases, such as the killing of a trans rough-sleeper by stabbing and earlier killings of gay men, indicate the risk is not confined to contested rural areas.

Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, placing Colombia ahead of most of the region on formal status; the divergence between that status and the homicide record is what the UN Independent Expert described as the gap between institutional progress and lived experience.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, a procedure opened by the June 2015 rule change. The official who defended that change described the earlier bodily inspections and psychiatric assessments as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

National identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025, and a comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025; its final status is not established in the sources.

The courts have intervened directly in detention. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

Residents face the same national homicide record as visitors: 270 LGBTIQ+ killings in 2025 against 164 in 2024, 35 LGBTI murders recorded by the Attorney General's Office between January and May 2025, and 13 trans people killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025.
